newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Bee Gees endure as fashions change.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bee Gees endure as fashions change.

text.p: If John Travolta can make a comeback, why can't the Bee Gees -- the band that helped propel him to big screen fame?

Of course the Bee Gees have never really gone away, just as Travolta insists he has been making "comebacks" ever since his Oscar-nominated turn 20 years ago as disco dancer Tony Manero in "Saturday Night Fever."

The brothers Gibb -- Barry, Robin and Maurice -- have continued recording and touring over the years. But nothing they have done has captured the public's imagination quite like the astonishing run of success they enjoyed in the second half of the 1970s, peaking in 1977 with the 40-million-selling soundtrack to "Saturday Night Fever."

In the 1980s their albums were overshadowed by the monster hits they effortlessly wrote and produced for others including Diana Ross' "Chain Reaction" and the Kenny Rogers/Dolly Parton duet "Islands in the Stream." Some of their more recent albums such as 1989's "One" and 1993's "Size Isn't Everything" did big business everywhere except the United States.
They are hoping to break that pattern with "Still Waters" (Polydor), which is riding high across Europe and comes out in the United States on May 6.
ROCK WORLD PAYS TRIBUTE

Coincidentally, that is the same day they are inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame during a ceremony at the museum's Cleveland home. Already this year they have been honoured at the American Music Awards in Los Angeles, the Brit Awards in London and the World Music Awards in Monte Carlo.

They caught their breath in Hollywood recently to talk about the album but the conversation frequently turned to other subjects such as the interesting home life of Robin Gibb, 47, the gaunt one, whose wife has a female lover.
"It takes the pressure off me. It's just a way of life," he said, explaining the advantages.

Or the long-discarded cocaine and booze habits of his twin brother, Maurice, rarely seen without a hat, who proudly sports an Alcoholics Anonymous lapel badge. "I'm more laid-back these days but I used to be a real terror," he said.
The idea of three brothers working together for more than 30 years and now living on the same street in Miami would drive a lot of people crazy.

"It's hard to be an individual," said Barry Gibb, 49, the best known of the three thanks to his falsetto voice and wavy locks. "We don't really hang out except when we're working. But we work so much that that's social for us too. So we don't need to go to each other's houses."
"We just hit the studio, which is up the road from the houses!" Maurice interjected.
"I think we've eventually come to terms with what we are and who we are, and this is our kind of music and that's it. There's no bigger picture than that," Barry added.
EVERY TRACK ITS OWN LITTLE WORLD

The "kind of music" is the ballad-heavy "Still Waters," which showcases the trio's trademark high-pitched harmonies. The album took 18 months to make, beginning with the first single, "Alone," in March 1995.
Maurice thinks there are at least six singles in the album. "Every track itself has got its own little world and the track before it doesn't sound like the last one."

But neither do any of the tracks appear to be cut from the same cloth as the group's hip-shaking hits such as "You Should Be Dancing," "Stayin' Alive," "Night Fever" or "Tragedy." This was deliberate, Maurice says, invoking one of the brothers' frequent references to their one-time peers, the Beatles: they too never went over old ground.

Which is more than can be said for the acts who jumped on the Bee Gees' bandwagon in the late 1970s with a slew of assembly-line disco songs. When the disco boom went bust at the end of the decade, everyone blamed the Bee Gees.
These days, it is safe to like disco again, and even though the Bee Gees never considered themselves a disco act they are benefiting from the revisionism.
DANCING TO 'FEVER' IN 2050

"The public today are rediscovering the music for themselves," Robin said, "and it has nothing to do with what the Bee Gees say or do. People will be dancing to 'Fever' in 2050. It's part of pop culture ... just as much as the Beatles, Buddy Holly and Evis Presley."

Helping the longevity will be a "Saturday Night Fever" stage show that one-time manager Robert Stigwood is putting together for a debut in London's West End next April. The Bee Gees wrote a new song, "Immortality," for it, and their 1968 hit "Words" has been resurrected.

The Bee Gees themselves will kick off a world tour in the United States in mid-September. They will tour Europe in the spring and hope to get to South America and South Africa for the first time in between.
"If you see our shows the array of audience is unbelievable," Maurice said. "Every time you have a new success you attract a new audience. Then they get interested in the back catalogue."
Immortality seems to be beckoning the Bee Gees.
